title: The Forgotten God
speaker: Pastor Lehman

outline.title: Forgetting God by Disregarding His Word
subpoints: Israel transgressed the covenant by rejecting God's authority.
The union between God and His Word means one cannot be remembered without the other.
Israel claimed to know God while rejecting 'the good' of covenant submission.

outline.title: The Mercy of the Trumpet
subpoints: The shofar signals impending judgment to allow for repentance.
God warns His people so they may be restored rather than destroyed.
This mirrors Christ's initial call to repent and believe the gospel.

outline.title: Living Autonomously
subpoints: Autonomy is living as one's own law, rejecting external divine claims.
Israel appointed kings and princes without God's acknowledgment.
Self-rule is the root of spiritual rebellion.

outline.title: Idolatry and False Worship
subpoints: Israel created idols from silver and gold, rejecting the true God.
The calf of Samaria represents a man-made substitute for divine presence.
Worshiping on one's own terms is a form of spiritual adultery.

outline.title: Divine Judgment on the Unrepentant
subpoints: Those who sow the wind reap the whirlwind; rebellion yields no fruit.
Israel is swallowed up among the Gentiles due to their separation from God.
God will punish sins and remember iniquity, sending fire upon fortified cities.

summary:
In this sermon, the pastor examines Hosea 8, focusing on the theme of Israel's failure to remember their Maker. The central argument is that forgetting God is not merely a lapse of memory but an active rejection of His covenant and Word. The text highlights the inseparable union between God and His Scripture, asserting that one cannot truly know God while disregarding His commands. Israel's claim to know God is exposed as hypocritical when contrasted with their lifestyle of rebellion and idolatry.

The sermon identifies four primary ways believers forget God: by not living according to His Word, by living autonomously as their own law, by making worship self-centered, and by inviting divine judgment through persistent sin. The pastor emphasizes the mercy inherent in God's warnings, symbolized by the blowing of the trumpet, which serves to call the people to repentance before judgment falls. This warning is likened to Christ's initial proclamation of the kingdom, urging listeners to repent and believe.

The address concludes with a stern warning against the consequences of spiritual autonomy, where individuals appoint their own kings and create idols of their own making. The imagery of sowing wind and reaping whirlwind underscores the futility of a life lived apart from God's provision and authority. Listeners are urged to examine their own lives for signs of forgetting God and to respond to the trumpet's call with genuine repentance and submission to divine authority.
